Active Outcome Reporting Bias: This refers to the systematic distortion of study results due to selective reporting of outcomes that favor a particular intervention, while omitting or downplaying outcomes that do not. 2. GRADE 2: Benefits and Harms of Traction Compared to No Intervention: There is no available evidence from clinical trials to evaluate the benefits and harms of traction therapy in community-dwelling adults, including older adults aged 60 years and above, with chronic primary low back pain (with or without leg pain) when compared to no intervention. 3. GRADE 3: Benefits and Harms of Traction Compared to Usual Care: The evidence regarding the benefits and harms of traction therapy in managing chronic primary low back pain in community-dwelling adults, including older adults, compared to usual care, is limited and inconclusive. 4. GRADE 4: Benefits and Harms of Traction as an Adjunct Therapy: The potential benefits and harms of using traction as an adjunct therapy for chronic primary low back pain in community-dwelling adults, including older adults, remain unclear due to insufficient evidence. 5. Therapeutic Ultrasound Overview: Therapeutic ultrasound is an electrophysical treatment modality that delivers energy to deep tissue sites via ultrasonic waves. It is hypothesized to increase tissue temperature and/or induce non-thermal physiological changes, which may alleviate symptoms such as pain and inflammation and promote or accelerate tissue healing. The treatment is typically delivered at intensities of 1 W/cm² to 3 W/cm², in either continuous or pulsed mode. 6. GRADE 1: Benefits and Harms of Therapeutic Ultrasound Compared to Sham Ultrasound: The evidence on the benefits and harms of therapeutic ultrasound in managing chronic primary low back pain in community-dwelling adults, including older adults, compared to sham ultrasound, is limited. The available studies show mixed results, with some favoring therapeutic ultrasound and others showing little to no difference. 7. Critical Outcomes for Chronic Low Back Pain Management: The critical outcomes considered for evaluating interventions in chronic low back pain include: Pain reduction Improvement in back-specific function/disability General functional improvement/disability Health-related quality of life Psychosocial functioning Social participation Adverse events reported in trials Changes in medication use Incidence of falls 8. GRADE 2: Benefits and Harms of Therapeutic Ultrasound Compared to No Intervention: There is insufficient evidence to determine the benefits and harms of therapeutic ultrasound in managing chronic primary low back pain in community-dwelling adults, including older adults, when compared to no intervention. 9. Risk of Bias in Studies: Many studies were downgraded due to high or unclear risks of bias. These biases include issues with random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of care providers, incomplete outcome data, selective reporting, co-interventions, and compliance with the intervention. 10. Inconsistency in Results: Some studies were downgraded due to considerable statistical heterogeneity (I² > 90%), with unexplained variability in results. For example, some studies showed little to no difference, while others demonstrated effects favoring the intervention. 11. Imprecision in Results: Many studies were downgraded due to wide confidence intervals, which were consistent with both the possibility of benefit and the possibility of no effect or harm. This imprecision was often compounded by a low number of participants. 12. Indirectness of Evidence: Some studies were downgraded due to indirectness, as they included only one study in a subgroup or were unclear if the findings were representative of all high-income or low/middle-income countries. 13. Follow-Up Times: The follow-up times in the studies varied, ranging from 2 to 12 weeks, with some studies not specifying the follow-up duration. 14. Judgments Based on GDG Experience: In the absence of sufficient evidence, judgments regarding the acceptability, feasibility, and equity of interventions were made based on the experience of the Guideline Development Group (GDG) members. 15. Summary of Evidence Limitations: The overall evidence base for non-surgical management of chronic primary low back pain in adults is limited by small sample sizes, high risk of bias, inconsistency, imprecision, and indirectness. These limitations highlight the need for more robust and well-conducted studies to inform clinical guidelines. This explanation provides a detailed and professional interpretation of the content, suitable for a medical audience.
